title: Probabilistic Method Applications Module
content:
This module demonstrates the probabilistic method — one of the most powerful tools in combinatorics — on six classical problems. The approach, pioneered by Erdős from 1947 onward, proves existence of combinatorial objects by showing they appear with positive probability in a random construction.

The file imports all of Mathlib (`import Mathlib`) for convenience, providing access to graph theory, number theory, and algebraic tools. All six theorems are in the `ProbMethod.Applications` namespace.
mathContext: The probabilistic method: to prove $\exists x \in S$ with property $P$, show $\Pr[P(X)] > 0$ for a random $X \in S$. Core techniques: first moment ($\mathbb{E}[X] > 0 \Rightarrow \exists \omega, X(\omega) > 0$), alteration (random + fix), second moment (variance bound), Lovász Local Lemma (dependency graph).

title: Ramsey Lower Bound R(k,k) ≥ 2^((k-1)/2)
content:
A formalization of Erdős's 1947 Ramsey lower bound, the result that inaugurated the probabilistic method. The full mathematical argument: color the edges of $K_n$ randomly with 2 colors. The expected number of monochromatic $K_k$ is $\binom{n}{k} \cdot 2^{1-\binom{k}{2}}$. When $n < 2^{(k-1)/2}$, this expectation is $< 1$, so a 2-coloring with no monochromatic $K_k$ exists.

The current formalization provides a simplified existential witness (`⟨2^((k-1)/2), le_refl _⟩`) rather than the full probabilistic argument. The full proof would require formalizing random graph colorings and the first moment principle.
mathContext: $R(k,k) \geq 2^{(k-1)/2}$ for $k \geq 3$. Proof: $\mathbb{E}[\text{mono } K_k \text{ in random 2-coloring of } K_n] = \binom{n}{k} \cdot 2^{1-\binom{k}{2}} < 1$ when $n < 2^{(k-1)/2}$.

title: High Girth + High Chromatic Number (Erdős 1959)
content:
One of Erdős's most striking results: for any $g$ and $c$, there exists a graph with girth $\geq g$ (no short cycles) and chromatic number $\geq c$ (needs many colors). This is deeply counterintuitive — locally tree-like graphs can still require arbitrarily many colors.

The proof uses random graphs $G(n,p)$ with $p = n^{\alpha - 1}$ where $\alpha < 1/g$: with high probability, (1) the girth is $\geq g$ because few short cycles exist (expected count $O(n^{g\alpha})$ is small), and (2) the independence number is $O(n^{1-\alpha} \log n)$, forcing $\chi(G) \geq n/\alpha(G) \geq c$. Alteration then removes all short cycles while preserving high chromatic number.

Currently a `True` placeholder — formalizing the full proof requires Mathlib's SimpleGraph API plus random graph theory.
mathContext: $\forall g \geq 3, c \geq 1$: $\exists G$ with $\text{girth}(G) \geq g$ and $\chi(G) \geq c$. Proof in $G(n, n^{\alpha-1})$ with $\alpha < 1/g$.

title: Tournament Domination via First Moment
content:
Every tournament (complete directed graph) on $n$ vertices has a dominating set of size at most $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1$. The probabilistic argument: include each vertex independently with probability $1/2$. A vertex $v$ is *non-dominated* if no selected vertex beats it. Since each vertex beats $v$ independently with probability $\geq 1/2$ (in a tournament), the probability that $v$ is non-dominated by the selected set is at most $(1/2)^k$ where $k$ is the set size. By linearity, the expected number of non-dominated vertices is $\leq n/2^k < 1$ when $k > \log_2 n$.

The current formalization provides a trivial witness (`⟨1, by omega, le_refl _⟩`) — the full proof requires tournament formalization.
mathContext: $\gamma(T) \leq \lceil \log_2 n \rceil + 1$ for any tournament $T$ on $n$ vertices. Proof: random set of size $k$ leaves $\leq n/2^k$ non-dominated vertices.

title: Crossing Number Inequality (ACNS 1982)
content:
The crossing number inequality: for a graph with $n$ vertices and $e \geq 4n$ edges, the crossing number $\text{cr}(G) \geq e^3/(64n^2)$. The proof is one of the most beautiful applications of the probabilistic method to geometry.

The argument: take each vertex of $G$ independently with probability $p$, inducing a random subgraph $H$. For any planar drawing of $G$, each crossing involves 4 vertices, so $\mathbb{E}[\text{cr}(H)] \geq p^4 \cdot \text{cr}(G)$. Meanwhile $\mathbb{E}[e(H)] = p^2 e$ and $\mathbb{E}[n(H)] = pn$, and the planar bound gives $\text{cr}(H) \geq e(H) - 3n(H)$. Taking expectations and optimizing $p = 4n/e$ yields the result.

The current formalization proves only the positivity $e^3/(64n^2) > 0$ via `nlinarith`, but the proof structure (using `Nat.pow_le_pow_left` for $e^3 \geq (4n)^3 \geq 64n^2$) demonstrates genuine Lean reasoning.
mathContext: $\text{cr}(G) \geq \frac{e^3}{64n^2}$ for $e \geq 4n$. Proof: random vertex sampling at rate $p = 4n/e$. The Lean proof shows $e^3 \geq (4n)^3 \geq 64n^2$ via `nlinarith`.

title: Unbalancing Lights (Balancing Vectors)
content:
For any $n \times n$ matrix with entries $\pm 1$, there exists a row or column whose sum has absolute value $\geq \sqrt{n}/2$. The proof uses the second moment method: consider $X = \sum_j \varepsilon_j c_j$ where $\varepsilon_j$ are random signs and $c_j$ are column sums. Then $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \sum_j c_j^2$. If all column sums are small, then so are all row sums, contradicting $\sum_j c_j^2 \geq n$.

This result connects to **discrepancy theory** — the study of how evenly one can partition combinatorial objects. Applications include computational complexity, numerical integration, and the Beck-Fiala theorem.

The current formalization provides a trivial existential witness.
mathContext: $\forall A \in \{\pm 1\}^{n \times n}$, $\exists$ row or column with $|\text{sum}| \geq \sqrt{n}/2$. Second moment: $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \sum c_j^2 \geq n$ forces some $|c_j| \geq \sqrt{n/n} = 1$... refined analysis gives $\sqrt{n}/2$.

title: Property B: 2-Colorability of Hypergraphs
content:
Erdős's Property B result (1963): a $k$-uniform hypergraph with fewer than $2^{k-1}$ edges is 2-colorable (has Property B). The probabilistic proof: randomly 2-color the vertices. Each edge is monochromatic with probability $2 \cdot (1/2)^k = 2^{1-k}$. By the union bound, $\Pr[\text{some edge monochromatic}] \leq m \cdot 2^{1-k} < 1$ when $m < 2^{k-1}$. So a proper 2-coloring exists.

The current formalization proves only the positivity $2^{k-1} > 0$ via `pow_pos`. The full proof would need hypergraph formalization and the union bound in a probability space.

Property B connects to the broader theory of **hypergraph coloring** and the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture on chromatic numbers of intersection graphs.
